--- title: "Repeat & package: loops, matrices, functions" subtitle: "The R Statistical Language · Session 3" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · The R Statistical Language · Session 3 knitr: opts_chunk: echo: true --- # Welcome back ## Where we left off {.inv} You can already *explore* a dataset: shape it with the pipe and `dplyr`/`tidyr`, and read it back with ggplot2's grammar. - the [pipe]{.green} `|>` and the `dplyr`/`tidyr` verbs (`filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`/`summarise`); - [base-R plots]{.green} and [ggplot2]{.amber}: histograms, scatters, facets, boxplots; - the [transform → plot → interpret]{.indigo} EDA loop. ::: {.callout-desc} **The move today.** Your EDA loop is full of moves you repeat: grouped summaries, reshapes, simulations. This session looks *underneath* them: we leave the tidyverse and work in base R, replacing copy-paste with loops, reaching into two dimensions with matrices, and turning the moves you repeat into reusable functions you keep. ::: ## Today's map {.inv} ::: {.session-arc}
1Foundations
2Explore your data
3Repeat & package
::: Session 3 is the **"repeat & package"** move of the course: stop doing by hand what R can do by itself: - [repeat & branch]{.green}: [loops]{.green} (`for`, `while`) and conditionals (`if/else`, `ifelse`); - [reach 2D]{.amber}: [matrices]{.amber}, the vector's 2D cousin, plus linear algebra and `apply`; - [package the logic]{.indigo}: [writing your own functions]{.indigo}, scope-aware, vectorised, tested. ::: {.callout-desc} **The thread.** The Monte-Carlo experiment ties the session together: we *loop* over thousands of samples, and we *package* that loop into one reusable, tested function. Matrices give us the two-dimensional structures the algebra often lives in. ::: # Loops and conditionals ## The problem loops solve {.inv} Often you want to repeat the same step on many things: - your function models ten species; - you average over 1000 simulations; - you transform every column of a table. You could copy-paste... or you let **R repeat for you**. ## `for` loops {.inv} Repeat a block a fixed number of times: the body runs once per value: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="01-for-loops.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} for (i in 1:5) { # i takes each value of the sequence in turn print(i^2) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 [1] 4 [1] 9 [1] 16 [1] 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} total <- 0 for (x in c(2, 4, 6, 8)) { # the body runs once per value total <- total + x } total ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 20 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} Afterwards `i` and `x` are normal variables: they still hold the loop's last value. ::: ## Pre-allocate for speed {.inv} Growing a vector inside a loop is slow. **Pre-allocate** the result first: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="02-preallocate.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 1000L # a numeric vector of n zeros out <- numeric(length = n) # character(length = n): character vector with n "" # logical(length = n): logical vector with n FALSE # integer(length = n): integer vector with n 0L # vector(mode = "list", length = n): list with n NULL for (i in 1:n) { out[i] <- rnorm(1) } par(bg = "white") hist(out) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} **Rule of thumb.** Decide the output's length *before* the loop, create the container, then fill slots by index (`out[i] <- ...`). This is much faster than `out <- c(out, ...)` inside the loop, a habit that matters once your data grows. ::: ## `while` loops {.inv} Repeat *while a condition holds*: useful when you don't know the number of steps in advance: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="03-while-loops.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1 while (x < 1000) { x <- x * 2 } x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1024 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Guard against infinite loops"} If the condition never becomes `FALSE`, the loop runs forever. Always add a safeguard, e.g.: ```r x <- 1 max_iter <- 10 counter <- 0 while (x < 1000 && counter < max_iter) { x <- x * 2 counter <- counter + 1 } ``` ::: ## Conditionals: `if` / `else if` / `else` {.inv} Branch on a condition: only **one** branch runs: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="04-if-else.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} score <- 82 grade <- if (score >= 90) { "A" } else if (score >= 80) { "B" } else { "C" } grade ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "B" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Long vectors break `if`"} `if` needs a *single* `TRUE`/`FALSE`: use `ifelse()` for vectors. ::: ## Element-wise choice: `ifelse` {.inv} For **vectorised** decisions, use `ifelse(condition, when_true, when_false)`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="05-ifelse.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} temps <- c(-2, 15, 28, 33) ifelse(temps > 25, "hot", "not hot") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "not hot" "not hot" "hot" "hot" ``` ::: ::: ::: It applies the branch *element-wise* to a whole vector: no loop needed. This is the idiomatic replacement for "for each value, choose one of two things". ::: {.paper-card} **`if` vs `ifelse`.** - Use `if/else` to choose *which block of code* runs once; - Use `ifelse` to map a *vector* to one of two values. Mixing them up is a classic beginner bug. ::: ## Which tool when? {.inv} ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} **`for`**: repeat a block a *known* number of times (loop over columns, pre-allocated slots). **`while`**: repeat *until a condition* flips (unknown count of steps). **`if/else`**: choose *one block of code* based on a condition. **`ifelse`**: map a *vector* element-wise to one of two values. **`*apply` family**: apply a function to each element (Session 1 lists, matrices below). ::: {.paper-card} Often the *cleanest* loop is no loop at all: vectorization, `ifelse`, or `lapply`/`vapply` are simpler than an explicit `for`. ::: ::: ## The `*apply` family: loop & apply {.inv} Say "**apply this function to every element**" instead of writing the loop by hand: ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="lapply.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6) lapply(l, mean) # a list back — keeps the original structure ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $a [1] 2 $b [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="sapply.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6) sapply(l, mean) # tries to simplify: a named vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a b 2 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="vapply.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} l <- list(a = 1:3, b = 4:6) vapply(l, mean, 0) # like sapply, but you promise the output type ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a b 2 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card .fragment fragment-index=3} The family you first met on lists in **Session 1** (and will meet again on matrices as `apply`, `MARGIN = ...`): - `lapply` always, - `sapply` when simple, - `vapply` when you want the guarantee. It's "loop, *then* apply" collapsed into one verb. ::: ## Your turn: loops & conditionals {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. `for` loop printing squares of `1:10`. 2. Loop-sum `1:1000`; confirm it equals `sum(1:1000)`. 3. Given `temps <- c(-5, 4, 12, 25, 31)`, use `ifelse` to label `"freezing"`…`"hot"` by thresholds of your choice. 4. **Monte-Carlo**: average 5000 samples of `rexp(30)` into a pre-allocated vector, then `hist()` it: bell-shaped despite the exponential source? :::
Lab 1: loops

Lab 1: loops (≈25 min). Continue in lab-1-loops.R. The Monte-Carlo in Q4 is our Central Limit Theorem by simulation: no theorem needed, just loops and histograms.

# Matrices ## What is a matrix? {.inv} A **matrix** is a *two-dimensional rectangular array* of **one type** (usually numeric): a vector folded into rows and columns. It's the **2D cousin of the vector**. ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="matrix.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} (m <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 4 7 10 [2,] 2 5 8 11 [3,] 3 6 9 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} m[2, ] # subset with [row, col], like a data frame ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 5 8 11 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(m) # length-2 vector with dimensions ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(m) # number of rows ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} ncol(m) # number of columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} **Key distinction.** A data frame is a *list of columns* (columns may differ in type); a matrix is *one vector in 2D* (single type). For tabular *data* with mixed types, prefer a data frame/tibble; reach for a matrix when you need **linear algebra**. ::: ## Building & reshaping {.inv} A matrix is just a vector with a `dim`(ension) attribute; you can build or reshape them freely: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="reshape.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # column-major fill (A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 3 5 [2,] 2 4 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # rbind: bind by row identical(A, rbind(1:3, 4:6)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # cbind: bind by column cbind(A, c(7, 8)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 3 5 7 [2,] 2 4 6 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # strip the dim -> back to a vector dim(A) <- NULL A ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Column-major by default"} `matrix()` fills **column by column** unless you pass `byrow = TRUE`. A classic source of "why is my matrix transposed?" surprises. ::: ## Arithmetic & recycling {.inv} Element-wise arithmetic works like it does on vectors, and **recycling** applies: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="matrix-arithmetic.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} (M <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 1 3 5 [2,] 2 4 6 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # scalar multiplies every entry M * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 2 6 10 [2,] 4 8 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # length-2 vector recycles down the COLUMNS M + c(10, 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [1,] 11 13 15 [2,] 22 24 26 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} **Watch the recycling axis.** A length-2 vector recycles along columns (down), not across: get this wrong and your standardisation silently miscalculates each column. ::: ## Linear algebra {.inv} Matrices exist to do **algebra**: matrix product, transpose, inverse, determinant: ::: {.codewindow} ::: {.editor .r name="01-matrix-algebra.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} (A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 2 1 [2,] 4 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} A %*% t(A) # matrix product ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 5 11 [2,] 11 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} t(A) # transpose ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 2 4 [2,] 1 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="02-matrix-algebra.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} solve(A) # inverse ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 1.5 -0.5 [2,] -2.0 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} (A <- matrix(c(2, 4, 1, 3), nrow = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [1,] 2 1 [2,] 4 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} det(A) # determinant ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} diag(A) # extract diagonal ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.editor .r .fragment name="03-matrix-algebra.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} eigen(A) # eigen decomposition ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` eigen() decomposition $values [1] 4.5615528 0.4384472 $vectors [,1] [,2] [1,] -0.3636591 -0.5392856 [2,] -0.9315321 0.8421229 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution .fragment title="`%*%` is not `*`"} - `A * B` is **element-wise**; - `A %*% B` is the **matrix product** (rows × columns). Absent the right dimensions, `%*%` errors, which is usually the clue you wanted a matrix, not a data frame. ::: ## Fold a data frame into a matrix {.inv} Any rectangular **numeric** block can be coerced to a matrix when algebra needs it: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="as-matrix.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} nums <- iris[, 1:4] # 150 x 4, all numeric head(nums, n = 9L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width 1 5.1 3.5 1.4 0.2 2 4.9 3.0 1.4 0.2 3 4.7 3.2 1.3 0.2 4 4.6 3.1 1.5 0.2 5 5.0 3.6 1.4 0.2 6 5.4 3.9 1.7 0.4 7 4.6 3.4 1.4 0.3 8 5.0 3.4 1.5 0.2 9 4.4 2.9 1.4 0.2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} M <- as.matrix(nums) # data frame -> matrix dim(M) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 150 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} class(M) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "matrix" "array" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} `as.matrix()` forces everything to **one type**: if any column is character, the whole matrix becomes character. Check `str()` before you coerce, and keep a real data frame for mixed-type data. ::: ## Row/column summaries & `apply` {.inv} Summarise along one axis with the `row*`/`col*` helpers, or generalise with `apply`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="matrix-apply.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} (M <- matrix(1:12, 3, 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [1,] 1 4 7 10 [2,] 2 5 8 11 [3,] 3 6 9 12 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # per row (MARGIN = 1) - see also rowSums(M) rowMeans(M) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5.5 6.5 7.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # per column (MARGIN = 2) - see also colSums(M) colMeans(M) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 5 8 11 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # standard deviation of each row apply(M, 1, sd) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.872983 3.872983 3.872983 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # range of each column apply(M, 2, \(x) max(x) - min(x)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 2 2 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} `apply(M, MARGIN, fun)`: `MARGIN = 1` goes down rows, `MARGIN = 2` across columns. It's `lapply`'s 2D sibling: a loop over one axis hidden inside a one-liner. ::: ## Standardise a matrix (full example) {.inv} Let's **standardize** (z-score) every column of a matrix, the machinery behind a real analysis: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="scale.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} M <- matrix(c(1, 100, 2, 200), 2, 2) mu <- colMeans(M) # mean of each column sig <- apply(M, 2, sd) # sd of each column Z <- sweep(M, 2, mu, "-") # subtract each column's mean Z <- sweep(Z, 2, sig, "/") # divide each column's sd ``` ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} colMeans(Z) # ~ 0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} apply(Z, 2, sd) # ~ 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} `sweep(M, MARGIN, vector, FUN)` applies a function across one axis, here subtracting a column mean. This is the pattern `scale(M)` automates; you now see what's underneath. ::: ## Your turn: matrices {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. Build `matrix(1:20, 4, 5)`; report `dim`, `rowSums`, `colMeans`. 2. Transpose it with `t()`; what happens to the dimensions? 3. `A <- matrix(c(4, 2, 1, 3), 2, 2)`: compute `A %*% solve(A)`; what should you get? `det(A)`? 4. Standardise the columns of `iris[, 1:4]` (as a matrix) so each column has mean 0, sd 1. Check with `colMeans` / `apply(., 2, sd)`. :::
Lab 2: matrices

Lab 2: matrices (≈20 min). In lab-2-matrices.R. Standardising by hand is the kind of thing you'll later hand to a function, which is exactly the next section.

# Writing custom functions ## Why functions? {.inv} ::: {.spread .spread-md .spread-evenly} Copy-pasting code is how bugs multiply. A **function** lets you: - name a block of logic so its *intent* is readable; - reuse it with different inputs; - fix a bug **once** instead of in every copy. Any analysis you do more than twice deserves a function. ::: ## Anatomy of a function {.inv} ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="function-anatomy.R"} ```r function_name <- function(arg1, arg2 = default) { result <- ... # body: work on the arguments return(result) # hands a value back } ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} - **name**: how you call it; - **arguments**: inputs (optionals get defaults); - **body & return**: code that runs & value handed back. ::: ## Scope: what the body sees {.inv} Variables created *inside* a function live **only there**: they don't leak out: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="scope.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- function(x) { internal <- x * 2 # exists only inside the call internal + 1 } g(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution title="Lexical scoping"} A function *can* see variables from the outside, but relying on that is fragile: pass everything it needs as **arguments**. Explicit inputs in, explicit output out, is what makes functions testable and reusable. ::: ## Functions wrap loops {.inv} The Monte-Carlo from the loops section is a loop crying out to be a function: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="monte-carlo.R"} ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} clt_sim <- function(n = 30, R = 5000) { means <- numeric(R) for (r in 1:R) means[r] <- mean(rexp(n)) means } par(bg = "white") hist(clt_sim()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](session-3_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} **The payoff.** The loop from "Your turn: loops" is now a *named, reusable, parameterisable* tool: `clt_sim(n = 100)` measures the same CLT with bigger samples, no copy-paste. ::: ## Vectorised functions & defaults {.inv} Most functions are **vectorised** when building upon vectorized functions; they work element-wise on vectors: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="vectorized-function.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clamp <- function(x, lo = 0, hi = 1) { ifelse(x < lo, lo, ifelse(x > hi, hi, x)) } clamp(c(-1, 0.5, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.0 0.5 1.0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} - `ifelse` in the body: the element-wise tool from earlier, and the vectorised `clamp` needs no loop at all; - Note the use of default arguments which makes the parameters optional. ::: ## When functions aren't vectorised: `Vectorize()` & `replicate()` {.inv} Built-in functions are usually vectorised, but your own (or a third-party) function may only accept **one scalar at a time**. Two loop-free helpers: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="vectorize.R"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # not vectorised: takes one date string parse_it <- function(x) strsplit(x, "-")[[1]][1] ``` ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # only the first is parsed parse_it(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "2024" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # wraps it => element-wise parse_all <- Vectorize(parse_it) parse_all(c("2024-05-01", "2024-06-15")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2024-05-01 2024-06-15 "2024" "2024" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} # repeat an expression R times replicate(4, mean(rexp(10))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9542195 0.8648132 0.9167770 0.8644224 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.paper-card} **Loops without loops.** `Vectorize()` turns a scalar-only function into a vector one; `replicate(R, expr)` re-runs an expression `R` times and collects results, the function-flavoured cousin of `for`/`sapply`. Works with any expression, not just a named function. ::: ## Functions compose into pipelines {.inv} The tidyverse pipes data through functions with `|>`: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="pipe.R"} ```r penguins |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> dplyr::summarize(avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g)) # wrap a computation in your own function and pipe right in avg_mass_by <- function(df, group) { df |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |> dplyr::group_by({{ group }}) |> dplyr::summarize(avg_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) } ``` ::: ::: {.paper-card} **`{{ var }}`** is the tidyverse "embrace" shortcut that passes a bare column name into a function cleanly. We'll rely on it, and on writing tidy functions, throughout the Reproducible Workflows course. ::: ## Test your functions {.inv} A good habit: check a function against a case you *already know the answer to*: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="test.R"} ```r stopifnot(all(clamp(c(-1, 0.5, 2)) == c(0, 0.5, 1))) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-desc} **Why it matters.** Writing one-line *assertions* (`stopifnot`) turns "trust me" into "checked automatically". You'll build on this with a proper testing framework in the Reproducible Workflows course. ::: ## Your turn: functions {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} 1. `zscore(x)` = `(x - mean(x)) / sd(x)`, tested on `c(1,2,3,4,5)`. 2. `mad_ratio(x)` = `mean(abs(x - mean(x))) / sd(x)`, tested on `rnorm(1000)`. 3. `describe(x)` → named list of `mean`, `sd`, `median`, `min`, `max`. 4. (Stretch) Wrap the matrices standardisation into `standardize_cols(M)` using `sweep`. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
